(p-682)Surah "Quraysh"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿For the covenant (of) Quraysh﴾. It is connected to His saying: "so let them worship" (the Lord of this House). He commanded them to worship Him because of their covenant of the two journeys. The fa' (so) entered here because the speech carries the meaning of a condition, meaning: "Indeed, the blessings of Allah upon them cannot be counted. If they do not worship Him for His other blessings, then let them worship Him for this one, which is a manifest blessing." Or it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: "So He made them like eaten chaff, for the covenant of Quraysh." That is, that destruction was for the sake of this covenant. This is like what is called tadmin (interlocking) in poetry, which is when the meaning of one verse depends on the preceding one in a way that cannot be correct without it. In the codex of Ubayy, the two are a single surah without separation. It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that he omitted the basmala between them. The meaning is that He destroyed the Abyssinians who had targeted them, so that people would hear of this and honor them greatly, so that security would be established for them in their journeys, and no one would dare to attack them. It was also said that the meaning is: "Be amazed at the covenant of Quraysh." In the reading "li-ilaf Quraysh" (with a shortened vowel), the reading is Shami, meaning: for the companionship of Quraysh. It was also said: it is said "aliftuhu ilfan wa ilafan" (I became familiar with him). "Quraysh" is the offspring of al-Nadr ibn Kinana. They named him by the diminutive of "al-qirsh," which is a huge creature in the sea that attacks ships and cannot be overcome except with fire; the diminutive is for magnification. They were named after it because of their strength and power, as a comparison to it. It was also said: (p-683) it derives from "al-qarsh," which means gathering and earning, because they were earners through their trade and their travel in the lands.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 106, verse 2:

﴿Their familiarity (with) the journey of winter and summer.﴾ He stated the familiarity in general terms, then replaced it with what is restricted by the two journeys, to magnify the matter of the familiarity and to remind of the great blessing in it. The word "riḥla" (journey) is in the accusative by "īlāfihim" as its direct object, and he intended "riḥlatay al-shitā' wa-l-ṣayf" (the two journeys of winter and summer), so he used the singular form, because there is no risk of confusion. The Quraysh had two journeys: they travelled in winter to Yemen and in summer to Syria, where they engaged in trade and commerce. In their two journeys they were secure, because they were the people of God's Sacred Precinct (ḥaram), so no one would attack them, while others were raided.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 106, verses 3–4:

﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ ﴿who has fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear﴾. The indefinite form in "jū'in" (hunger) and "khawfin" (fear) is used to indicate their intensity, meaning: He fed them through the two journeys from a severe hunger they had been in before them, and He made them safe from a great fear, namely the fear of the People of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched away (al-takhattuf) in their land and on their travels. It is also said: they had been struck by a severe hardship, to the point that they ate carrion and burnt bones, and He made them safe from the fear of leprosy (al-judham), so that it would not afflict them in their land. It is also said: all of that was by the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).
